tool.name: Helm
tool.tagline: The package manager for Kubernetes: install, configure and upgrade apps as charts
tool.description: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into versioned, configurable charts and manages installed releases with upgrades and rollbacks. It is how most third-party software (databases, ingress controllers, monitoring stacks) is installed on clusters, and a common way to ship your own services.

glossary.def: A Helm package: a folder of Kubernetes manifests written as fill-in-the-blanks templates, plus default settings. Helm fills in the blanks and installs the result as one app.
One installed copy of a chart in a cluster, with its own name, settings and history. The same chart can be installed as several releases.
One numbered version of a release. Every install, upgrade or rollback adds a revision, which is how Helm can show history and go back to an earlier state.
In Helm, a place on the web where charts are published for others to download, like a shelf in an app store. (A git repository is something else: a project folder with its full history of changes.)
A container image registry, such as Docker Hub or GitHub's, used to store charts as well as images. OCI is the shared standard these registries follow.
The public website for finding charts that others have published, with links to the repositories that hold them.
A YAML file of settings for a chart. The chart's own values.yaml holds the defaults; files you pass with -f replace some of them for your install.
Combining two sets of nested settings by going inside each group and changing only the names that are mentioned, instead of replacing the whole group.
The tool most teams use to record every change to their project files, with who made it and why, so any earlier version can be seen or restored.
A popular add-on for Helm that shows, line by line, what an upgrade would change in the cluster before you run it.
A step that changes how a database stores its data, such as adding a column, run when a new version of an app needs it. It usually isn't undone automatically.
The fill-in-the-blanks language Helm templates are written in, taken from the Go programming language: ordinary text with {{ }} placeholders that Helm replaces with values.
Information Helm hands to every template, such as .Values (the settings), .Release (its name and namespace) and .Chart (details from Chart.yaml).
A large collection of ready-made template functions (for text, numbers, lists, dates and encoding) that Helm adds to its template language.
A reusable snippet of template, defined once with define (usually in _helpers.tpl) and inserted wherever it's needed with include.
A chart that another chart (its parent) includes as a dependency. It is installed together with the parent, as part of the same release.
A chart holding only shared template snippets for other charts to use. It can't be installed on its own.
A chart with no templates of its own, only other charts as dependencies, used to install a whole set of apps as one release.
In Helm, an object (usually a Job) marked with the helm.sh/hook annotation. Helm runs it at a set moment, such as just before an upgrade, instead of applying it with the rest of the release.
A hook marked as a test, usually a small pod that checks the installed app answers. helm test runs a release's chart tests.
A quick check, right after installing or deploying, that the basics work (say the app answers at all), before relying on it or testing deeper.
A tool that checks Kubernetes manifests against the official description of every kind of object, without needing a cluster, catching misspelled or wrongly typed fields.
A Helm add-on for writing small automatic tests of a chart: given certain values, check that the rendered manifests contain what you expect. It needs no cluster.
A tool for checking charts in automated builds: it lints the charts that changed, installs them into a temporary cluster and checks that their version was raised.
A small, throwaway Kubernetes cluster made by the kind tool, which runs each node as a Docker container. Popular for tests in automated builds.
A signature file (.prov) Helm can create next to a packaged chart, so users can check who published the chart and that it hasn't been changed since.
A tool from the Sigstore project for signing images and charts stored in registries, and for checking those signatures before use.
Helm 3's way of upgrading: it compares the previous release's manifest, the new one and the live object, and changes only what the chart itself changed.
Differences that creep in between what you declared (in git or a chart) and what actually runs, for example after someone edits an object by hand.
A popular GitOps tool: it runs in the cluster, watches git and applies the manifests it finds there, showing what differs in a web dashboard.
A popular GitOps tool: controllers in the cluster that keep it matching git, including a helm-controller that installs and upgrades Helm releases.
A program Helm passes the rendered manifests to just before applying them, so you can change them (often with Kustomize) without editing the chart.

concepts.name: What Helm is: charts, releases, repos
concepts.summary: Helm installs a whole app on Kubernetes from one package, a chart; each install is a release you can upgrade or undo.
concepts.why: These three words (chart, release, repository) appear in every Helm command and every chart's instructions.
concepts.body:
Think about what it takes to run a real app on Kubernetes: a Deployment for its pods, a Service so others can reach them, a ConfigMap and a Secret for settings, maybe an Ingress for outside traffic. That's five or more manifests, and every team that installs the app needs slightly different settings in them.

**Helm** solves this the way an app store does on your phone. Someone packages all those manifests once; you install the package with one command and change only the settings you care about. A **package manager** is a program that downloads and installs ready-made packages like this, and Helm is the package manager of Kubernetes.

A **chart** is the package: a folder holding the app's manifests written as templates (files with blanks to fill in), a file of default settings called `values.yaml`, and `Chart.yaml`, which gives the chart's name and version. For sharing, a chart can also be packed into a single `.tgz` file, much like a zip file.

A **release** is one installed copy of a chart in your cluster, with a name you choose. Install the same Redis chart twice, as `redis-cache` and `redis-sessions`, and you get two independent releases. Helm keeps a history of every change to a release, which is what lets you upgrade it and roll it back.

A **repository** is where charts are published for others to download, like a shelf in the app store. Some are classic websites with an `index.yaml` file listing their charts. Others are an **OCI registry**: the same kind of registry that stores container images (OCI is the standard those registries follow). To find public charts, search **Artifact Hub**, a website listing charts from many repositories.

Helm runs only on your computer or in your CI/CD system; nothing of it is installed in the cluster. It **renders** the chart, meaning it fills in the templates' blanks with your settings to produce ordinary manifests. Then it sends them to the API server, logging in with your kubeconfig just as kubectl does, and saves each release's history as Secrets in the release's namespace.

Helm 4, released in late 2025, uses the same chart format as Helm 3, so charts work with both. The differences are mostly in commands and add-ons.
concepts.code:
helm version
# version.BuildInfo{Version:"v4.0.0", ...}

helm search hub postgresql | head -3        # search Artifact Hub
helm list -A                                # releases in all namespaces
# NAME        NAMESPACE  REVISION  STATUS    CHART             APP VERSION
# monitoring  obs        7         deployed  kube-prometheus-stack-77.0.0  v0.85.0

# Helm's history of that release, stored as Secrets in its namespace
kubectl get secrets -n obs -l owner=helm
# sh.helm.release.v1.monitoring.v7   helm.sh/release.v1   ...
takeaways: Chart = the package, release = one installed copy, repository = where charts are published
Helm runs on your machine and keeps each release's history as Secrets in the cluster
One chart can be installed many times, as separate releases

quiz.q: You install the same Redis chart twice with different names. What do you have?
options: An error: a chart installs once per cluster
quiz.explain: Each install with a new name creates a separate release of the same chart.

quiz.q: Where does Helm keep the history of a release?
options: In a Helm server running inside the cluster
Only in a folder on your laptop
In Secrets in the release's namespace
quiz.explain: Helm has no part running in the cluster; it stores each release's history as Secrets next to the release.

concepts.name: Installing charts from repos and OCI
concepts.summary: Add chart repositories, search them, and install, inspect and remove releases.
concepts.why: This is how most ready-made software, from databases to dashboards, gets installed on a cluster.
concepts.body:
For a classic repository, you tell Helm about it once: a short name of your choice and its web address (its **URL**). Helm then downloads the repository's list of charts, so searching works without going online each time:

- `helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts`, then `helm repo update`, which fetches the latest list.
- `helm search repo prometheus` searches the repositories you've added; `--versions` lists every version.
- `helm show values prometheus-community/prometheus` prints the chart's default settings, its values. Read them before installing: they're how you'll configure the app.

Charts in an OCI registry need no `repo add`; you point at them directly with an `oci://` address: `helm install cache oci://registry.example.com/charts/redis --version 1.2.0`.

Installing:

- `helm install <release> <chart> -n <ns> --create-namespace` installs a chart as a release in a namespace, creating the namespace if needed.
- Always pin the chart version with `--version`. Without it you get whatever is newest, which can change between today and next week.
- `helm upgrade --install` installs the release if it doesn't exist yet and upgrades it if it does. Running it again is safe (it's idempotent), which is why automated CI/CD jobs use it.
- `--wait` makes Helm wait until the new pods are ready, and `--timeout 10m` sets how long it may wait before giving up with an error (a **timeout**).

Inspecting and removing:

- `helm list -n ns` lists releases; `helm status <release>` shows a release's state plus the chart's usage notes.
- `helm get manifest <release>` shows the manifests Helm actually applied, and `helm get values <release>` the settings you supplied.
- `helm uninstall <release> -n ns` deletes the release's objects and its history. Storage claimed by StatefulSets (their PVCs) is usually left behind on purpose, so data isn't lost by accident.

Before relying on a public chart, check that its publisher still looks after it; charts do get abandoned or moved.
concepts.code:
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm search repo prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack --versions | head -3

helm show values prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack > defaults.yaml

helm upgrade --install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --version 77.0.0 -n obs --create-namespace --wait --timeout 10m

helm status monitoring -n obs
helm get manifest monitoring -n obs | grep -c '^kind:'   # count the objects it created
helm uninstall monitoring -n obs
takeaways: helm repo add + update for classic repositories; oci:// addresses need no add
Always pin --version; use upgrade --install in automation
helm get manifest / values shows what a release really contains
pitfalls: Leaving out --version, so a later run silently installs a much newer chart that behaves differently.

quiz.q: Which command is safe to run again and again in CI/CD, whether or not the release already exists?
quiz.explain: upgrade --install creates the release the first time and upgrades it on every later run.

concepts.name: Configuring with values
concepts.summary: Change a chart's default settings with values files and --set, and learn how Helm combines them.
concepts.why: Every chart is configured through values, and the combining rules decide what your release really gets.
concepts.body:
A chart's values are its settings: how many replicas, which image tag, whether to create an Ingress. The chart ships defaults in its `values.yaml`. You replace the ones you want to change when you install or upgrade; replacing a default with your own value is called **overriding** it.

The usual way is a **values file**: a YAML file with just your changes, passed with `-f my-values.yaml` (or `--values`). You can pass several. Helm combines them in order and later files win, so a common pattern is `-f base.yaml -f prod.yaml`: shared settings first, then production's.

For a single setting, use `--set` in the terminal: `--set image.tag=1.5.0`. Dots walk into nested settings (the `tag` inside `image`). For an item of a list, give its position in square brackets, counting from zero: `--set ingress.hosts[0]=a.example.com`. `--set` beats every `-f` file.

Two smaller flags: `--set-string` keeps a value as text, so `--set-string tag=1.10` stays `1.10` instead of becoming the number 1.1. `--set-file key=path` reads a value from a file, such as a certificate.

How combining works. YAML groups settings in two ways: a map is a set of `name: value` lines (like `image:` with `repository` and `tag` inside), and a list is lines starting with `- `. Maps are **deep-merged**: Helm goes inside and changes only the names you mention, so you write only the settings you change. Lists are **replaced** whole: to change one item, you must repeat the entire list. Setting a name to `null`, YAML's word for "nothing", removes a default.

Keep your values files in **git**, the tool most teams use to record every change to their project files, and prefer them to long chains of `--set`. Files can be reviewed, and they give the same result every time.

On upgrade, `helm upgrade` without values goes back to the chart's defaults, quietly undoing your settings. Helm has flags to carry the previous values over (`--reuse-values`), but then what runs no longer matches what's in git. Pass the same values files on every upgrade instead.

`helm get values <release> --all` shows the combined result Helm used.
concepts.code:
# prod.yaml
replicaCount: 3
image:
  tag: "1.5.0"          # deep-merged: image.repository keeps its default
resources:
  requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi}
ingress:
  enabled: true
  hosts:                # lists are replaced entirely
    - host: shop.example.com
      paths: [{path: /, pathType: Prefix}]
# helm upgrade --install shop ./shop -n shop -f values-base.yaml -f prod.yaml \
#   --set image.tag=1.5.1      # --set wins over both files
# helm get values shop -n shop --all
takeaways: -f files combine in order, later ones winning; --set beats them all
Maps deep-merge; lists are replaced whole
Pass the same values files on every upgrade instead of reusing old values
pitfalls: Overriding one entry of a list in values and silently losing the other default entries.

quiz.q: Defaults have image: {repository: nginx, tag: 1.26}. Your file sets image: {tag: 1.27}. What is image.repository?
quiz.explain: Maps are deep-merged, so repository keeps its default.

quiz.q: base.yaml sets replicaCount: 2, prod.yaml sets 3, and you run helm upgrade -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml --set replicaCount=5. How many replicas?
options: An error: the value is set twice
quiz.explain: Later files beat earlier ones, and --set beats every file.

concepts.name: Upgrades, history and rollbacks
concepts.summary: Upgrade releases, inspect their revision history and roll back to a previous revision.
concepts.why: Changing running software safely, and undoing it fast, is Helm's main value after install.
concepts.body:
Every `helm upgrade` creates a new **revision** of the release: a numbered record of the rendered manifests and the values used. Helm then applies the differences to the cluster. Objects that disappeared from the chart are deleted; new ones are created.

- `helm history shop -n shop` lists revisions with their status (`deployed`; `superseded`, meaning replaced by a later one; `failed`) and a description.
- `helm rollback shop 4 -n shop` re-applies revision 4's manifests as a **new** revision (say 7), so history is never rewritten.
- `helm upgrade ... --wait` waits until the new pods are ready. Add `--rollback-on-failure` (called `--atomic` in Helm 3) and an upgrade that fails or runs out of time is rolled back automatically.

Two ways to look before you leap. `--dry-run=server` renders the chart and has the API server check the result, without changing anything. The **helm-diff** plugin (a **plugin** is an add-on you install into a program) adds `helm diff upgrade ...`, which shows line by line what would change, like `kubectl diff`.

Limits to remember:

- A rollback restores Kubernetes objects, not data. If the new version changed how its database stores data (a **database migration**), rolling back doesn't undo that.
- `helm rollback` changes the cluster but not your values files in git. Fix git too, or the next automated deploy upgrades again.
- If a release is stuck in `pending-upgrade` after an interrupted run, roll back to the last good revision before upgrading again.
- `--history-max` (default 10) limits how many revisions are kept.
concepts.code:
helm upgrade shop ./shop -n shop -f prod.yaml --wait --timeout 5m
helm history shop -n shop
# REVISION  STATUS      CHART       APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
# 5         superseded  shop-1.3.0  1.4.2        Upgrade complete
# 6         deployed    shop-1.4.0  1.5.0        Upgrade complete

helm rollback shop 5 -n shop --wait
helm history shop -n shop --max 1
# 7         deployed    shop-1.3.0  1.4.2        Rollback to 5

# one-step safety net in CI (Helm 4 flag name)
helm upgrade --install shop ./shop -n shop -f prod.yaml --rollback-on-failure --timeout 5m
takeaways: Each upgrade or rollback is a new revision
Rollback restores objects, not data or your git
--wait plus --rollback-on-failure is a cheap safety net for automated deploys
pitfalls: Expecting a rollback to undo a database migration that the new version already ran.

quiz.q: After rolling revision 6 back to 4, what revision number is now deployed?
quiz.explain: A rollback creates a new revision with revision 4's content.

concepts.name: Anatomy of a chart
concepts.summary: Learn the files of a chart: Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/, helpers, NOTES.txt and .helmignore.
concepts.why: You need to read charts you install and write charts for your own services.
concepts.body:
`helm create shop` builds a small working chart for you to start from. Each part has a job.

`Chart.yaml` describes the chart. It has `apiVersion: v2`, a `name`, and two version numbers that are easy to mix up. `version` is the version of the **chart** itself; raise it every time you change anything in the chart. `appVersion` is the version of the app it installs, for information only.

Chart versions follow **semantic versioning**: three numbers, `major.minor.patch`, like `1.4.0`. Raise the last for fixes, the middle for new features, and the first when users must change something to upgrade. `Chart.yaml` can also give the chart's `type` (`application`, or `library` for shared helpers only) and list other charts it needs under `dependencies`.

`values.yaml` holds the default settings, with comments explaining each one. Think of it as the chart's control panel: it's the part users are meant to touch, so keep it tidy and documented.

`templates/` holds the manifests, written as templates. The blanks are marked with double curly braces, like `{{ .Values.replicaCount }}`, which Helm replaces with a setting. Every file here is rendered into a manifest, except files whose names start with `_` (like `_helpers.tpl`): those hold reusable snippets.

`templates/NOTES.txt` is rendered and printed after an install, usually with tips on how to reach the app. `charts/` holds other charts this one needs. `values.schema.json` (optional) lists the allowed settings and their types, so Helm can reject wrong ones. `.helmignore` lists files to leave out of the package.

`helm template shop ./shop -f prod.yaml` renders the chart on your machine and prints the finished YAML, without touching a cluster: the best way to see what you'll get. `helm package ./shop` packs the folder into `shop-1.4.0.tgz`.

Keep the chart next to the code of the app it installs (in a `chart/` or `deploy/` folder). Delete the files `helm create` made that you don't use; a smaller chart is easier to look after.
concepts.code:
helm create shop
tree shop
# shop/
#   Chart.yaml  values.yaml  .helmignore  charts/
#   templates/  _helpers.tpl  deployment.yaml  service.yaml  ingress.yaml
#               hpa.yaml  serviceaccount.yaml  NOTES.txt  tests/

cat shop/Chart.yaml
# apiVersion: v2
# name: shop
# type: application
# version: 0.1.0
# appVersion: "1.16.0"

helm template shop ./shop --set replicaCount=2 | grep -A2 'kind: Deployment'
takeaways: version = the chart's version (raise it on every change); appVersion = the app's
Files starting with _ hold helpers and aren't output as manifests
helm template renders locally so you can read the result
pitfalls: Changing templates without raising the chart version, so two different packages share one version number.

quiz.q: Which field must change when you modify a chart's templates and publish it?
quiz.explain: version identifies the chart package itself; appVersion describes the deployed app.

concepts.name: Templates, values and built-in objects
concepts.summary: Fill templates with .Values, .Release and .Chart, and transform values by passing them through template functions.
concepts.why: Templates turn one chart into many configurations, and most chart mistakes are template mistakes.
concepts.body:
Helm templates are written as **Go templates**, the fill-in-the-blanks language that comes with Go (a language for writing programs, which Helm itself is written in), with extra helpers added. Everything outside `{{ }}` is copied as it is; whatever is inside `{{ }}` is worked out and its result put in its place.

Inside the braces, a path starting with a dot reads information. Helm hands every template a few **built-in objects**:

- `.Values`: the combined values.
- `.Release.Name`, `.Release.Namespace`, `.Release.IsUpgrade`, `.Release.Revision`: about this release.
- `.Chart.Name`, `.Chart.Version`, `.Chart.AppVersion`: from `Chart.yaml`.
- `.Capabilities.KubeVersion`, `.Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "policy/v1"`: what the cluster supports.
- `.Files.Get "conf/app.conf"`: reads an ordinary file shipped in the chart.

To transform a value, you call a **function**: a named action that takes a value and gives back a new one. `quote` wraps a value in double quotes, `upper` turns it into capitals, and `default "web"` gives back `"web"` when the value is empty. Helm includes **Sprig**, a collection of dozens of such functions, plus a few of its own.

A **pipeline** chains functions with `|`, passing each result on to the right, like a **pipe** in the shell: `{{ .Values.name | default "web" | quote }}` takes the name, falls back to `web` if it's empty, then quotes it. Other common ones: `toYaml` (turn a setting into YAML text), `nindent` (indent it), `required` (stop with a message if it's missing), `b64enc` (base64-encode) and `printf` (build text from pieces).

Build names from the release (`{{ .Release.Name }}-web`), so several releases of the chart can live in one namespace without clashing.

Indentation is the classic trap. YAML uses indentation to show what's inside what, but Helm treats a template as **plain text** and knows nothing about that. When inserting a block of YAML, indent it yourself: `toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12` puts the block on a new line, indented 12 spaces. `{{-` and `-}}` remove the spaces and **line breaks** on that side of the braces, which keeps the output tidy.

A useful trick: put a **checksum** of the ConfigMap in an annotation on the pod template. `sha256sum` computes a short fingerprint of the text, which changes whenever any character of the ConfigMap changes. A changed annotation changes the pod template, so a settings change rolls out new pods.
concepts.code:
# templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-web
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount | default 1 }}
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}}
      annotations:
        # fingerprint of the rendered ConfigMap: a settings change rolls the pods
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
takeaways: .Values, .Release, .Chart, .Capabilities and .Files are the built-in objects
Pipelines pass a value through functions: value | function | function
toYaml ... | nindent N inserts YAML blocks with the right indentation
pitfalls: Forgetting quote on values like "yes" or "1.10", which YAML would otherwise read as true or as the number 1.1 instead of as text.

quiz.q: What does {{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }} produce when image.tag is empty?
quiz.explain: default gives back the value written after it whenever the value piped into it is empty.

concepts.name: Control flow and named templates
concepts.summary: Use if, with, range and variables, and share snippets with define, include and _helpers.tpl.
concepts.why: Optional features need if-blocks, and label blocks repeated in every file need reusable snippets.
concepts.body:
Templates can make decisions and repeat things. Three blocks cover almost everything, each closed by `{{ end }}`.

`{{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }} ... {{ else }} ... {{ end }}` outputs the first part only when the value counts as true. False, 0, empty text, empty lists and maps, and missing values all count as false; everything else counts as true. Combine tests with `and`, `or`, `not` and `eq` (equals).

`{{ with .Values.nodeSelector }} ... {{ end }}` outputs its block only if the value isn't empty. Inside the block, the dot `.` means that value, which saves repeating the long path.

`{{ range .Values.hosts }} ... {{ end }}` repeats its block once for each item of a list, with `.` set to the current item: a **loop**. `{{ range $key, $val := .Values.env }}` goes through a map instead, in alphabetical order of names.

A **variable** keeps a value under a name starting with `$`: `{{ $name := .Release.Name }}`. One variable is always there: `$` on its own means the top level, the same thing `.` meant at the start of the file. Because `with` and `range` change what `.` means, write `$.Release.Name` inside them.

**Named templates** stop you copying the same lines into every file. Define one in `templates/_helpers.tpl` with `{{- define "shop.labels" -}} ... {{- end }}`, then insert it anywhere with `{{ include "shop.labels" . | nindent 4 }}`.

Start every template name with the chart's name. Template names are shared by a chart and every chart it includes, so two charts that both define `labels` would overwrite each other. Use `include` rather than the older `template` action: `include` gives back text you can pipe into `nindent`.

The `.` after the name is what the snippet gets to see. `include "x" .` passes the current dot; inside a `range`, pass `$` instead, or bundle several values into a small map with `dict`.
takeaways: if / with / range; empty values count as false; $ is the top level inside with and range
define in _helpers.tpl, insert with include ... | nindent
Start template names with the chart name
pitfalls: Using .Release.Name inside a range block, where the dot is the current item; use $.Release.Name.

quiz.q: Inside {{ range .Values.hosts }}, how do you reach the release name?
quiz.explain: range sets the dot to each item in turn; $ always means the top level.

concepts.name: Chart dependencies and subcharts
concepts.summary: List the charts your chart needs in Chart.yaml, configure those subcharts through values, and switch them on or off.
concepts.why: Shipping a database with your app, or a whole stack in one install, is built from dependencies, and their values rules trip people up.
concepts.body:
A chart can include other charts: your shop chart can bring a PostgreSQL database along, for example. The included charts are its **dependencies**, also called **subcharts**; your chart is their parent. List them in `Chart.yaml` under `dependencies`, each with:

- `name` and `version`, where the version can be a range such as `~16.4.0` (any 16.4.x).
- `repository`: a repository URL, an `oci://...` address, or `file://../common` for a folder next to yours.
- optionally `condition`, `tags` and `alias`, described below.

`helm dependency update` downloads them into `charts/` and writes `Chart.lock`, a **lock file** recording the exact version chosen for each one. `helm dependency build` downloads exactly those versions again later. Commit `Chart.lock` to git so every build gets the same subcharts.

- Settings for a subchart go under its name (or alias) in the parent's values: `postgresql.auth.database: shop`.
- `condition: postgresql.enabled` lets users switch the subchart off, for example to use a database run by their cloud company in production.
- `alias` lets you include the same chart twice under different names.

Who sees what: a subchart sees only its own section of the values, never the parent's. The one way round this is `global`: anything under `.Values.global` is shared with every subchart. A parent can read a subchart's values, not the other way round.

Reusable template snippets (named templates, made with `define`) work across charts: a name defined in one chart can be used in all of them. That is what makes a **library chart** possible: a chart holding only shared snippets, which other charts list as a dependency.

An **umbrella chart** has no templates of its own, only dependencies: a popular way to install a whole stack as one release. But one release also means one upgrade for everything, and one bad change can break all of it at once, so keep umbrellas small.
concepts.code:
# Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: shop
version: 1.4.0
appVersion: "1.5.0"
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "~16.4.0"
    repository: oci://registry.example.com/charts
    condition: postgresql.enabled

# values.yaml
postgresql:
  enabled: true
  auth: {database: shop, username: shop}
global:
  imageRegistry: registry.example.com   # visible to all subcharts

# helm dependency update ./shop   -> charts/postgresql-16.4.x.tgz + Chart.lock
takeaways: Declare in Chart.yaml, run helm dependency update, commit Chart.lock
Configure a subchart under its name; global is shared with all of them
condition and tags switch subcharts on and off
pitfalls: Expecting a subchart template to read the parent's top-level values.

quiz.q: How can a value be seen by both the parent chart and all its subcharts?
options: Put it at the top level of values.yaml
quiz.explain: Only .Values.global is passed down to every subchart.

concepts.name: Hooks and chart tests
concepts.summary: Run Jobs at set moments of an install or upgrade with hooks, and check a release works with helm test.
concepts.why: Running database migrations before an upgrade, and quick checks after it, are common release steps.
concepts.body:
A **hook** is an ordinary template, usually a Job, carrying the annotation `helm.sh/hook`. Instead of applying it with the rest of the release, Helm runs it at a chosen moment:

- `pre-install`, `post-install`, `pre-upgrade`, `post-upgrade`, `pre-delete`, `post-delete`, `pre-rollback`, `post-rollback`, and `test`.

Helm waits for a hook's Job or pod to finish before it continues, and a failed hook fails the whole operation. To order several hooks, set `helm.sh/hook-weight` (lower runs first).

Hook objects are **not** part of the release, so Helm won't clean them up for you. Set `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy`: `before-hook-creation` deletes the old one just before running it again (the usual choice); `hook-succeeded` and `hook-failed` delete it after it succeeds or fails.

The typical use is a `pre-upgrade` Job that runs the database migration with the new image before any new pod starts. Make migrations **backward compatible**, meaning the old version of the app still works with the changed database: old pods keep running during the rollout, and a rollback won't reverse the migration.

One catch: `pre-install` hooks run before the release's ConfigMaps and Secrets exist. A hook that needs them must create its own, or run `post-install` instead.

**Chart tests** are hooks marked `helm.sh/hook: test`, usually a pod that sends one request to the app's Service and fails if no good answer comes back. `helm test shop -n shop` runs them whenever you like, which makes an easy **smoke test**, a quick does-it-basically-work check, right after a deploy.

GitOps tools translate Helm hooks into their own mechanisms, not always identically; check before relying on unusual combinations of hooks.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-migrate
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 1
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          args: ["migrate", "--to", "latest"]
          envFrom: [{secretRef: {name: {{ .Values.db.secretName }}}}]
# helm upgrade shop ./shop --wait   -> Job runs and must succeed first
# helm test shop                    -> runs templates annotated "helm.sh/hook": test
takeaways: helm.sh/hook annotations run objects at set moments of the release
Hooks aren't part of the release: set a delete policy
helm test runs test hooks as a smoke test after a deploy
pitfalls: Migrations that break the old version of the app, which is still running during the rollout.

quiz.q: Why add hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation to a migration Job hook?
options: So the previous Job is removed and the hook can be created again on the next upgrade
quiz.explain: Job names are reused; deleting the old one first avoids an 'already exists' failure.

concepts.name: Linting, schemas and testing charts
concepts.summary: Catch chart mistakes before they reach a cluster with helm lint, a values schema, checks on the rendered output and helm-unittest.
concepts.why: Otherwise template mistakes show up during real deploys; charts deserve tests like any code.
concepts.body:
Several layers of checking, cheapest first. Each runs in seconds on your machine or in CI/CD.

`helm lint ./shop -f prod.yaml` is Helm's **linter**: a tool that reads files looking for likely mistakes, without installing anything. It checks the chart's structure, renders the templates and flags common errors. Run it once with each environment's values file.

A **schema** describes what valid settings look like: which ones exist, their types, which are required. Put one in `values.schema.json`, written in **JSON Schema**, the standard format for describing JSON data. Helm checks the values against it on install, upgrade, lint and template, rejecting typos and wrong types with a clear message.

Make the schema strict: list the settings that must be given under `required`, set `additionalProperties: false` so unknown names are rejected, and use `enum` to allow only a fixed list of values.

Inside templates, `{{ required "image.tag is required" .Values.image.tag }}` stops rendering with your message when a setting is missing.

`helm template ... | kubeconform -strict` checks the rendered manifests against Kubernetes' own description of every kind of object, offline. Policy tools such as conftest or the Kyverno CLI check your own rules on them, such as "every container sets CPU and memory limits".

**helm-unittest** is a Helm **plugin** (an add-on installed into Helm) for **unit tests** of charts: small automatic checks that, given certain values, the output looks right, for example "the Deployment has 3 replicas". It needs no cluster and runs in seconds.

**chart-testing** (`ct lint`, `ct install`) lints the charts you changed and installs them into a throwaway **kind cluster**, a small Kubernetes cluster that runs inside Docker containers. It also checks that each changed chart's version was raised.

A sensible CI/CD setup for a git project full of charts: lint, schema, unit tests and kubeconform with each values file, then install into a kind cluster and run `helm test`.
takeaways: Run helm lint and helm template with each environment's values
values.schema.json rejects bad values before anything is applied
helm-unittest for fast checks of the output; chart-testing plus a kind cluster for real installs
pitfalls: Writing a schema but leaving additionalProperties open, so typos like replicaCont still pass.

quiz.q: A user sets replicaCount: "three". What stops this at install time?
options: A values.schema.json declaring replicaCount as an integer
quiz.explain: Helm validates values against the schema on install and upgrade and rejects the wrong type.

concepts.name: Packaging and publishing to OCI registries
concepts.summary: Package charts, push them to OCI registries, sign them, and version them with SemVer.
concepts.why: Sharing charts across teams or publicly means publishing versioned packages that others can check haven't been tampered with.
concepts.body:
Today the usual place to publish charts is an OCI registry: GitHub's (ghcr.io), Docker Hub, your cloud company's registry (Amazon ECR, Azure ACR, Google's), or a self-hosted Harbor. Charts sit next to your images, behind the same logins and access rules.

- `helm registry login ghcr.io -u USER --password-stdin` logs in; `--password-stdin` reads the password from the previous command's output (see the code), so it isn't typed into the command itself.
- `helm package ./shop` produces `shop-1.4.0.tgz`. The version comes from `Chart.yaml`; `--version` and `--app-version` override it in CI/CD.
- `helm push shop-1.4.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts` stores it as `ghcr.io/acme/charts/shop:1.4.0`: the chart version becomes the tag.
- Users install with `helm install shop oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/shop --version 1.4.0`, or list it as a dependency with that address as its repository.

Classic chart repositories (an `index.yaml` plus `.tgz` files, often hosted on GitHub Pages with the chart-releaser tool) still work. But the `index.yaml` file must be rebuilt on every release and downloaded whole by every user, while OCI registries need nothing extra.

Versioning: follow semantic versioning for the chart version. A **breaking change** to the values, one that forces users to edit their values files (a renamed or removed setting), means raising the first number. Explain what users must change in the chart's **README**, the introduction file shipped with it, or in a changelog.

Signing lets users check that a chart is exactly what you published. Helm's built-in `--sign` and `--verify` use a **provenance file** (`.prov`) signed with a PGP key. Many teams instead use **cosign**, from the Sigstore project, to sign the pushed chart in the registry and check the signature before installing.

Every pushed chart also gets a digest, the `sha256:...` fingerprint of its exact contents. A tag like `1.4.0` can be pushed again with different contents; a digest can't. Referring to a chart by digest therefore pins it **immutably**: it can never change under you.
concepts.code:
# CI gives a token; --password-stdin reads it from echo, not from the command line
echo "$GITHUB_TOKEN" | helm registry login ghcr.io -u acme-bot --password-stdin

helm package ./shop --version 1.4.0 --app-version 1.5.0
# Successfully packaged chart and saved it to: shop-1.4.0.tgz

helm push shop-1.4.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts
# Pushed: ghcr.io/acme/charts/shop:1.4.0
# Digest: sha256:9c1e...

helm show chart oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/shop --version 1.4.0
cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/charts/shop@sha256:9c1e...   # sign by digest
takeaways: Package, then push to oci://registry/path; install with --version
OCI registries need no `index.yaml` file
Use semantic versioning for charts; sign them (cosign) and pin by digest
pitfalls: Re-pushing a changed chart under an existing version tag, so consumers get different content for the same version.

quiz.q: What determines the version tag a chart gets when pushed to an OCI registry?
options: The chart version from Chart.yaml (or --version when packaging)
quiz.explain: The packaged chart's version becomes the OCI tag.

concepts.name: How Helm applies changes and stores releases
concepts.summary: Where Helm keeps release records, how it merges changes (three-way merge or server-side apply), which objects it owns, and drift.
concepts.why: Stuck releases, 'invalid ownership' errors and fights with other tools over the same setting all come from these mechanics.
concepts.body:
**Release storage.** Each revision is a Secret named `sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<revision>` in the release's namespace, labelled `owner=helm`. Inside is the whole release (chart, values, rendered manifests, status), squeezed smaller (**compressed**) with gzip and then base64-encoded. So anyone allowed to read Secrets in that namespace can read your values, passwords included. Helm can keep releases elsewhere (`HELM_DRIVER=configmap`, or `sql` for a database), and `--history-max` limits how many records pile up.

**Ownership.** Helm labels and annotates everything it creates (`app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm`, `meta.helm.sh/release-name`, `meta.helm.sh/release-namespace`). Installing a chart that contains an object which already exists without these marks fails with an "invalid ownership metadata" error. Adding the marks by hand lets Helm **adopt** the object: take it over as part of the release. The annotation `helm.sh/resource-policy: keep` makes Helm leave an object in place on uninstall, useful for storage claims (PVCs).

**Applying changes.** Others may change objects Helm created: an autoscaler raising `replicas`, a person adding an annotation with kubectl. Helm 3 copes with a **three-way merge**: it compares the previous release's manifest, the new one and the live object, and changes only what the chart changed, so other people's edits to fields Helm never set survive.

Helm 4 uses Kubernetes' **server-side apply** for new releases instead: the API server does the merging and records which tool owns each field. When two tools set the same field, for example a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (the object that changes replica counts automatically) owning `replicas` while your chart sets it too, you get an explicit conflict instead of a silent tug-of-war.

**Drift.** Helm compares only against what it rendered last time; it never watches the cluster or puts manual edits back. Differences that creep in this way are called **drift**, and correcting it continuously is what GitOps controllers do.

**CRDs.** A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) adds a new kind of object to the cluster, such as `Certificate`. Charts often ship CRDs in a `crds/` folder. Helm installs those once and, on purpose, never upgrades or deletes them, because changing or removing a CRD can delete every object of that kind across the cluster. Manage CRD upgrades separately.
concepts.code:
# decode a release record: base64 twice (Kubernetes, then Helm), then gunzip
kubectl -n shop get secret sh.helm.release.v1.shop.v7 -o jsonpath='{.data.release}' \
  | base64 -d | base64 -d | gunzip | jq '{name, version, status: .info.status, values: .config}'
# {"name":"shop","version":7,"status":"deployed","values":{"image":{"tag":"1.5.0"}}}

# adopt an existing object into a release
kubectl -n shop annotate svc shop-web meta.helm.sh/release-name=shop \
  meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=shop
kubectl -n shop label svc shop-web app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=Helm

# which tool owns which fields (server-side apply)
kubectl get deploy shop-web -n shop --show-managed-fields -o yaml | grep 'manager:'
takeaways: Release revisions are compressed Secrets: limit who can read them
Ownership annotations decide what Helm manages; resource-policy: keep leaves objects behind
Helm 3 three-way merge vs Helm 4 server-side apply; CRDs in crds/ are never upgraded
pitfalls: Assuming Helm will put manual kubectl edits back to the chart's state on its own.

quiz.q: Why does upgrading a chart not update the CRDs in its crds/ folder?
options: CRDs belong to the whole cluster, so Helm can't touch them
Helm deliberately installs crds/ only once, to avoid destructive CRD changes
quiz.explain: Changing a CRD can delete data across the whole cluster, so Helm leaves CRD upgrades to you.

concepts.name: lookup, tpl and library charts
concepts.summary: Read live cluster objects with lookup, treat values as templates with tpl, fail with clear errors, and share helpers via library charts.
concepts.why: Large collections of charts, and the platform teams behind them, rely on these to avoid copy-paste and stay correct.
concepts.body:
Powerful functions, each with a catch:

- `lookup "v1" "Secret" .Release.Namespace "shop-db"` reads a live object from the cluster while rendering, for example to keep a generated password the same across upgrades instead of making a new one each time. With no cluster to ask, as under `helm template` or `--dry-run=client`, it returns an empty map, so templates must handle that case. It also makes the output depend on what's in the cluster, which GitOps tools often can't provide.
- `tpl .Values.annotationsTemplate .` renders a text value as a template, so users can write `{{ .Release.Name }}` inside their values. Handy, but values full of template code soon become hard to read.
- `fail "message"` and `required` stop rendering with a clear error when values don't make sense together, such as an Ingress switched on with no hosts listed.
- `dict`, `list`, `merge`, `mergeOverwrite`, `deepCopy`, `toJson` and `fromYaml` build and combine maps and lists, so a helper can take several inputs at once and build whole objects.

**Library charts** (`type: library` in `Chart.yaml`) contain only named templates and can't be installed. Application charts list one as a dependency and call its helpers, for example `{{ include "common.deployment" (dict "root" . "name" "api") }}`. Platform teams use this to give dozens of services identical labels, probes and security settings while each service's own chart stays tiny.

Keep charts boring: templating everything leads to a chart nobody can maintain. If you need real logic, write a small program (in Python or Go, say) that generates the manifests, or use an operator.
takeaways: lookup reads live objects but is empty during helm template
tpl renders values as templates; fail/required give clear errors
Library charts share helpers across many service charts
pitfalls: Relying on lookup in a chart deployed by a GitOps tool that renders without cluster access, so the password is regenerated every time it renders.

quiz.q: What does lookup return when you run helm template without a cluster?
quiz.explain: helm template has no cluster connection, so lookup returns an empty map.

concepts.name: Helm with GitOps and post-renderers
concepts.summary: Deploy charts with Argo CD or Flux, patch rendered output with post-renderers, and decide which tool owns the release.
concepts.why: At scale, charts are deployed by controllers from git, not by people typing helm upgrade.
concepts.body:
With GitOps, a controller in the cluster keeps the cluster matching git, undoing drift as it goes. The two major GitOps tools both accept Helm charts, but use them differently:

- **Flux** runs real Helm operations through its helm-controller, driven by `HelmRelease` objects. Releases show up in `helm list`, hooks and history behave as in Helm, and Flux can roll back failed upgrades automatically.
- **Argo CD** renders the chart, like `helm template`, and applies the output itself. There's no Helm release: Argo tracks the objects and their drift on its own, maps hooks onto its own sync phases (the ordered steps of one deploy), and `lookup` has no cluster to read.

So choose knowingly: charts that depend on release history, `lookup` or unusual hooks behave differently under Argo CD.

A **post-renderer** changes the rendered manifests after templating and before applying, without forking the chart (making and maintaining your own modified copy of it): `helm install --post-renderer ./kustomize-wrapper`. In Helm 4, post-renderers are provided as plugins. The usual approach passes the YAML into Kustomize to add labels, sidecars or patches that the chart's values don't offer. Flux supports Kustomize post-renderers directly in `HelmRelease`.

Moving a change from staging to production then becomes a git change: raise the chart version or change values in the staging folder, check it, then do the same in production's folder. Pair this with a values schema (a description of the allowed settings, which Helm enforces) and rendering checks in CI/CD, so broken values never reach the cluster.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata: {name: shop, namespace: shop}
spec:
  interval: 10m                 # re-check git and the cluster every 10 minutes
  chart:
    spec:
      chart: shop
      version: "1.4.x"
      sourceRef: {kind: HelmRepository, name: acme-charts}
  values:
    replicaCount: 3
  upgrade:
    remediation: {retries: 2}   # roll back after failed upgrades
  postRenderers:                # patch the rendered Deployment without forking the chart
    - kustomize:
        patches:
          - target: {kind: Deployment, name: shop-web}
            patch: |
              - {op: add, path: /spec/template/metadata/annotations/team, value: payments}
takeaways: Flux runs real Helm releases; Argo CD renders and applies itself
Post-renderers patch output without forking charts
Promote by changing versions/values in git
pitfalls: Moving a chart to Argo CD without checking its use of lookup and hooks.

quiz.q: Under Argo CD, why might helm list show no release for an app deployed from a chart?
options: Argo CD renders templates and applies manifests itself rather than running helm install
The chart is a library chart
Releases are stored in another namespace
quiz.explain: Argo CD uses Helm only as a renderer; it manages the resources directly.
